fundamental.thesis: Tata Power is India's largest integrated power utility — spanning thermal generation (Mundra), renewables (4+ GW operational, TP Solar manufacturing), and T&D distribution in Mumbai/Delhi — and is structurally positioned at the intersection of India's energy-transition and electrification themes. Q1FY27 revenue grew 5.6% YoY to ₹19,051 cr with PAT up 11.0% YoY to ₹1,401 cr (7.4% PAT margin), representing a meaningful acceleration from the -1.8% revenue trough of 9MFY26 — EBITDA margin expanded to 23.6% from 21.2% YoY driven by a high-margin renewables segment (32.1% EBITDA margin) and T&D revenue surging 13.5% YoY; TP Solar's 2GW H1FY27 output milestone further validates the manufacturing flywheel. Using EV/EBITDA of 15.23× as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive hybrid (the sector card explicitly calls for EV/EBITDA over P/E), Tata Power sits at the 26th percentile vs broad-market peers and 34.7% below the median — fairly valued to modestly cheap — though the trailing P/E of 34.41× far exceeds the 10–18× utilities sector benchmark, an artefact of high financial leverage (D/E 168×) and a renewable-growth premium embedded in the equity. The single biggest risk is a USD 490 million (≈₹4,100 cr) contingent SIAC arbitration liability (Kleros Capital NDA breach) with no provision recorded — an adverse ruling would effectively erase roughly three full quarters of PAT and could necessitate dilutive equity issuance against an already stretched balance sheet.

Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. It is a power-and-metals cyclical, not a regulated utility like NTPC or POWERGRID. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,212 cr, up only 1.6% YoY. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. The big QoQ jump (PAT +144%) mostly recovers from a weak Q4, helped by higher plant load factors (India 85.4%, Zambia 89.3%), and does not mark a new uptrend. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 10.0x EV/EBITDA, 1.79x P/B and 20.9x trailing P/E, the stock sits in the bottom quartile of the broad market (P10 on EV/EBITDA, P14 on P/B), but its P/E is above the 10–18x utilities band. Once you allow for Zambia country risk and cyclical earnings, I'd call it fair rather than clearly cheap. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

fundamental.thesis: Vodafone Idea is the third and weakest player in India's telecom market, which has roughly 2.5 players. It runs on a large government-linked debt and dues structure and is trying a capex-led turnaround while Jio and Airtel hold most of the industry's revenue. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 6.0% YoY to ₹11,689 cr, up from +1.9% in Q3FY26, and EBITDA margin rose to 43.1% from 42.5%; ARPU climbed 10.2% YoY to ₹195 and subscribers grew for the first time since the merger (193.1 mn), but the PAT loss was still ₹3,754 cr, a -32.1% margin, after ₹5,120 cr of finance costs and ₹5,467 cr of D&A. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive telecom. On that basis the stock is expensive: 28.6x versus the card's 9–12x norm for Indian mobile operators, 63rd percentile against the broad market, and the price sits at 90% of its 52-week range. The 4.3x trailing P/E is meaningless because a one-off FY26 gain distorts it, book value is negative, and the forward P/E is also negative. The biggest risk is solvency: negative net worth of ₹38,327 cr, deferred spectrum and AGR dues of about ₹1.56L cr with ₹9,259 cr due by June 2027, and a turnaround that depends on lender support and ₹45,000 cr of capex. The Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov are a near-term event risk.

fundamental.thesis: Indus Towers rents mobile tower space to telecom operators, with about 2.7 lakh towers and 1.63 tenants per tower in the latest KPI data. Revenue growth slowed from +7.9% in Q3 FY26 to +4.6% in Q1 FY27 and +4.0% (₹8,516 cr) in Q2 FY27, while PAT growth went from +0.5% to -2.5% (₹1,793 cr), leaving H1 PAT down 1.6% at ₹3,519 cr; I treated the row labelled Q2FY26 as Q2 FY27 because H1 less Q1 revenue is exactly ₹8,516 cr, but the same subtraction gives PAT of ₹1,773 cr and the 55.3% H1 EBITDA margin sits above both quarters (53.6% and 54.4%), so the margin figures are only approximate. On EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive businesses, 8.12× is below its 9-12× range, which is written for mobile operators rather than tower companies, so I grade the stock cheap, helped by a 15.29× trailing P/E and H1 free cash flow of ₹4,332 cr, though the bottom-quartile peer ranks are against the broad market rather than true peers and slowing growth justifies part of the discount. The biggest risk is a major customer under AGR-related stress that is paying only monthly billings, which has already kept ₹198 cr of revenue unrecognised in H1, while the 13.31× forward P/E assumes roughly 15% EPS growth even as PAT falls and estimates are being cut (FY EPS -1.4% over 90 days); leverage is also unclear, because the reported 2.33× net debt/EBITDA does not reconcile with debt of about ₹21,000 cr implied by the 53% debt/equity, or roughly 1.1× annualised EBITDA.

fundamental.thesis: ITI Limited is a Government of India-owned telecom equipment manufacturer (PSU under Department of Telecommunications) engaged in defence communication, broadband gear, and telecom network products — a structurally impaired business currently in a BIFR-supervised revival plan, NOT a telecom service operator and therefore the Telecom sector card (ARPU/EBITDA framework) does not apply here. Revenue declined -14.6% YoY in Q1 FY27 (₹425 cr vs ₹498 cr), continuing a severe multi-quarter deceleration that saw -39.5% over 9MFY26 and -32.2% over H1FY26; PAT remains deeply negative at -₹32 cr (-7.4% margin), though marginally better than -₹64 cr a year ago — the 'PAT margin expanding' trajectory signal is misleading as it simply reflects a slightly smaller loss on a shrinking revenue base. Valuation is strikingly expensive: trailing P/E of 79.4× sits at P87 among 473 broad-market peers (+126% premium to market median of 35.2×) and EV/EBITDA of 483× is economically meaningless for a loss-making entity — the ₹25,371 cr market cap is pricing in the ₹8,280 cr ASCON Phase IV defence order optionality and GoI backing, not current earnings power. The single biggest risk is the material audit qualification — auditors issued a disclaimer of opinion citing Ind AS 115 revenue recognition failures on complex engineering contracts, inventory obsolescence, and inadequate internal controls, which means reported numbers cannot be relied upon and could be restated downward.

fundamental.thesis: Phoenix Mills is India's dominant organised retail mall operator (not primarily a residential developer) — its Property & Related Services segment runs ~57% EBITDA margins on a portfolio of high-footfall malls, making it closer to a retail REIT-annuity than a cycle-linked developer. Per the sector card, P/E is structurally meaningless for real estate; using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for this capital-intensive model), PHOENIXLTD trades at 28.3× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P62 rank, +21% premium) — fairly valued given the annuity-quality mall revenues, but not cheap, and the premium leaves no margin of safety against balance-sheet stress. The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

Mahanagar Gas is the dominant city gas distributor in Mumbai, Thane and Raigad, supplying CNG to vehicles and piped gas to homes and businesses, so its earnings depend on the gap between what it pays for gas and what it can charge customers. Sales are growing but profit is shrinking. H1FY27 revenue rose 18.5% YoY to Rs 5,377 cr, while PAT fell 35.7% to Rs 328 cr. By our calculation, Q2FY27 revenue was about Rs 2,778 cr (+23% YoY) and PAT about Rs 135 cr (about -29% YoY), the third straight period of shrinking margins: EBITDA margin fell from 20.6% in 9MFY26 to 14.3% in Q1 and 12.7% in H1. Because this is a capital-intensive, regulated-style utility, we graded valuation on EV/EBITDA (7.4x) and P/E (14.2x trailing, 12.9x forward), both inside the 10-18x Utilities / Energy range, so we call it fair. The low multiple reflects the margin squeeze and should not be read as a bargain; the broad-market peer rank is a fallback with no true gas-distribution peers and carries little weight. The biggest risk is that gas costs keep rising faster than prices, given cuts to cheaper domestic gas allocation, more costly gas in the mix and crude near $91.

fundamental.thesis: NHPC is India's largest hydropower generator, a government-owned company that earns a regulated return on the power plants it has commissioned, so its profits grow with commissioned capacity rather than with power prices; the Subansiri Lower project (1,250 MW of a planned 2,000 MW now running) is its main growth driver. In H1 FY27, revenue grew 26.0% YoY to ₹8,291 cr and PAT grew 20.6% to ₹2,836 cr (PAT margin 34.2%), faster than the +14.5% revenue growth a year earlier; however, ₹918 cr of that revenue is provisional Parbati-II income still awaiting CERC tariff approval, finance costs more than doubled (+115%), and EBITDA margin fell from 65.7% to 63.0%. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive utilities, NHPC trades at 25.5x, slightly above the broad-market median of 23.3x; its trailing P/E of 27.4x is well above the 10–18x utilities range, and a P/B of 1.85x against an ROE of only 9% is not cheap, so I grade it expensive on current earnings. The low forward P/E of 11.9x (estimates raised 3.9% over 90 days) and the stock sitting near the bottom of its 52-week range are the main counterpoints. The biggest risk is that heavy borrowing (net debt about ₹56,700 cr, debt/equity 1.36, negative free cash flow) keeps pushing up interest costs faster than new capacity adds earnings, especially if the remaining Subansiri units are delayed or the Parbati-II provisional revenue is cut when CERC sets the tariff.

fundamental.thesis: Prestige Estates is a Bangalore-anchored, multi-city branded developer with residential, office, retail and hospitality arms, and it is one of the larger listed players in the consolidating RERA-era sector. H1 FY27 reported revenue was flat at about ₹4,735 cr (-0.1% YoY), down from +72.7% growth in FY26. PAT fell 31.4% to ₹528 cr (11.2% margin), the owners' share fell 36.4%, and EBITDA was down 5.7% as land, contractor and finance costs rose. One caveat: reported P&L here trails bookings by 2-4 years, and the Q2 pre-sales and collections figures from the Oct-13 operational update were not in the extracted data, so I cannot assess the metric that matters most for a developer. Using EV/EBITDA and P/B+ROE rather than P/E (55x trailing is not meaningful for developers), the stock looks roughly fair. EV/EBITDA of 21.6x sits about 7% below the broad-market median, but a 4.0x P/B for an 8% ROE is rich, and with the stock at 60% of its 52-week range the margin of safety is limited. The CPPIB hospitality deal (₹15,000 cr first tranche closed Oct 2026, up to ₹30,000 cr committed) and strong H1 operating cash flow (₹1,311 cr, CFO/PAT 2.5x) are real positives. Against them, debt/equity is about 1.05x and consensus EPS has been cut 7-11% over 90 days even though 19 of 21 analysts rate it a buy, which is a classic pre-derating pattern.

Using P/E and EV/EBITDA as the yardsticks, the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E of 52.15x is above the sector card's 18-30x OEM range and 92.3% above the peer median, forward P/E of 30.1x is at the top of that range and the highest among peers, and EV/EBITDA of 22.53x is at P83; a rough filings-based trailing P/E near 36x would still be expensive, and I disregarded the implausible 35% dividend yield and 47x P/B and the consensus upside, whose implied price of about Rs 4,304 conflicts with about Rs 3,370 from the 52-week position and market cap. The biggest risk is that a premium valuation leaves little room for error if margins keep slipping while cash conversion stays weak, with H1 operating cash flow of only Rs 358 cr after Rs 3,352 cr of financing-arm loan disbursements and net debt up from Rs 2,159 cr to Rs 3,470 cr.

fundamental.thesis: ICICI Lombard is one of India's largest private general insurers, with about 10.3% of the motor market and a fast-growing health book (retail health +64% YoY), offset by a shrinking commercial lines segment (-8.1%). In H1 FY27, gross direct premium rose only 5.4% YoY to Rs 15,110 cr (gross premium written +9.6% to Rs 16,562 cr) while PAT fell about 14% to Rs 1,350 cr, because the claims ratio worsened from 72.3% to 77.4%, the expense ratio rose to 74.5% and the combined ratio reached 107%, so profits now lean on investment income. Judged on the insurer yardstick of price-to-book against return on equity (not P/E or EV/EBITDA), a P/B of 5.45x for a ROE of 15.5-17.9% is expensive: the stock sits at the 91st percentile of financials on P/B and the 79th on trailing P/E (31.8x vs a 17.5x median), and the forward P/E of 23.8x assumes an earnings rebound that analysts have been trimming (-3% FY EPS revisions over 90 days). The biggest risk is that claims inflation in motor and health keeps the combined ratio above 105% and the expected rebound never arrives, which would leave little room to justify the premium multiple.

Per the official filings, Q2FY27 revenue rose +30.0% YoY to ₹3,802 cr and PAT rose +44.0% to ₹409 cr, a clear acceleration from Q1FY27's +14% revenue and +16% PAT (the pre-computed 'decelerating' label reads the rows in reverse order; the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹2,586 cr does not match the PDF and is ignored). PAT margin improved to 10.8% from 9.4% and EBITDA margin to 16.3%, while the order backlog of ₹23,646 cr (+58% YoY, about 6.2x sales) on order intake of ₹8,485 cr (+78% YoY) gives more than two years of revenue visibility. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names for order-book industrials, the stock trades at 90.2x against a peer median of 34.0x (P100 in sector), with trailing P/E at 122x and forward P/E at 68x, at 97% of its 52-week range; that is clearly expensive even after allowing for the electricals premium. The biggest fundamental risk is weak cash conversion (H1 CFO/PAT of 0.43x, FCF of -₹290 cr, receivables up ₹788 cr) combined with widening semiconductor losses (₹84 cr in H1), at a valuation that leaves no room for an execution slip or a capex-pause de-rating.

H1 FY27 revenue was 29,435 cr and PAT 7,670 cr, against 29,731 cr and 8,877 cr in H1 FY26, which I compute as -1.0% and -13.6% (the trend table shows -1.8% and -11.6%, possibly from a restated base, unverified); revenue growth has slowed from +11.8% in H1 FY26 to roughly flat and PAT margin has fallen from 29.8% to 26.1%, while the implied average quarterly PAT of about 3,835 cr is above the implied Q4 FY26 figure of 3,388 cr but below Q3 FY26's 4,043 cr. fundamental.thesis: InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) is India's largest airline, with a 442-aircraft fleet, and its results are driven mainly by fares, fuel costs and the rupee rather than the order-book measures in the Industrials sector card. Q2FY27 revenue growth accelerated over the available periods from +4.7% in Q1FY26 to +25.9% (Rs 23,364 cr), but this was fare-led (yield +34.3%) while passengers fell 4.7% and load factor fell 2.2 points to 80.3%; the Rs 1,879 cr net loss narrowed from Rs 2,582 cr, including about Rs 1,155 cr of forex losses, with unit revenue (Rs 5.76) still below unit cost (Rs 6.22) and fuel cost per unit up 68.9%. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick because trailing P/E is unavailable on losses, valuation is fair rather than cheap: 16.4x is 51.7% below the 34.0x peer median and forward P/E is 21.0x, but those peers are mostly capital-goods and auto companies, the forward multiple relies on a recovery while current-year EPS estimates have been cut 18.9% in 90 days, and P/B of 27.1x is the highest in the group. The biggest risk is that crude (USD 96.61 and rising) and a weak rupee keep costs above fares while softer passenger demand limits further fare increases, although Rs 39,929 cr of free cash provides a cushion against Rs 87,303 cr of debt including leases; the H1FY27 PAT and margin figures do not reconcile with Q1 and Q2, so this view relies on the quarterly numbers.

fundamental.thesis: Bosch India (BOSCHLTD) is a domestic-content auto ancillary and technology supplier — a wholly-owned subsidiary of Robert Bosch GmbH — producing fuel injection systems, chassis systems (expanded via RBIC acquisition July 2026), powertrain and beyond-mobility solutions across PV, 2W, CV, and off-highway segments in India. Q1FY27 revenue grew +22.0% YoY to ₹5,842 cr, accelerating from +9.4% in Q3FY26, led by automotive (+25.7%), power solutions (+29.0%), and a standout two-wheeler segment (+41.4% on premium EMS platforms); however, reported PAT fell -36.7% YoY to ₹706 cr (PAT margin 12.1%) purely due to a ₹556 cr exceptional gain in the base quarter — normalised PAT growth is approximately +5%, modest, and the 'Others' segment revenue declined 22.8%, signalling beyond-mobility weakness. At trailing P/E of 39× against an 18–28× sector benchmark and EV/EBITDA of 39× that ranks at P100 in the peer group (104.8% premium to sector median of 19.1×), Bosch is expensive using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for this capital-intensive business, even allowing for its quality premium as a global technology subsidiary. The biggest risk is RBIC integration — financed at ₹90,238 million (~₹9,024 cr) that has pushed D/E to 0.8 — which could pressure margins and debt serviceability if auto demand softens under a RISK_OFF macro with rising crude.

Indian Oil is India's largest state-run refiner and fuel marketer, so its earnings depend on government fuel-pricing policy as much as on crude prices: falling crude helps it, rising crude hurts. H1FY27 revenue rose 28.4% YoY to ₹549,972 cr and PAT rose 35.2% to ₹21,362 cr, but the half was very uneven: Q1 was a loss (₹-1,141 cr; EBITDA margin 1.9%), then Q2 PAT jumped to about ₹21,630 cr as refining margin (GRM) rose from $15.59 to $18.52/bbl. Revenue growth looks driven mostly by price rather than volume, since marketing sales fell from 26.2 to 25.2 MMT quarter-on-quarter and diesel sales from 10.9 to 9.0 MMT. On the yardstick the sector card names for oil marketing companies (P/E plus dividend yield, EV/EBITDA as a cross-check), the stock looks low on trailing numbers: P/E 4.4x against a peer median of 9.2x, EV/EBITDA 4.1x against 6.1x, and P/B 0.85x with 21% ROE. Those trailing numbers are inflated by an unusually strong Q2, though. Q3FY26 (latest extracted official data) showed revenue of ₹3,427 cr (+40.4% YoY) and PAT of ₹464 cr (+1,040% YoY off a severely depressed Q3FY25 base of ₹82 cr), with PAT margin expanding from 6.4% (Q3FY25) to 13.5% (Q3FY26) and GNPA improving from 2.4% to 1.6% — but Q2FY27 results filed October 15 remain unextracted, leaving a ~9-month data gap that materially limits current visibility. On the appropriate lender yardstick (P/B + ROE), IIFL trades at 1.62× P/B with a 12.3% ROE — borderline cheap — confirmed by a P11 broad-market percentile rank on trailing P/E and a forward P/E of 7.66× (vs trailing 13.65×) that implies strong consensus earnings growth priced in at a meaningful discount to NBFC sector median of 18–28×. The biggest fundamental risk is governance: the re-designation of co-founder R Venkataraman from Joint MD to Non-Executive Director on October 15 is a leadership change at a sensitive recovery juncture, compounded by a declining Provision Coverage Ratio (114% in Q3FY25 to 63% in H1FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT −7.34×), all of which limit conviction despite the appealing valuation.

LIC is India's dominant life insurer, with a 58.8% share of first-year premium income (37.5% in individual policies, 70.5% in group) and ₹59.6L cr of assets under management. In H1FY27, gross premium income grew 11.6% YoY to ₹2,75,423 cr, up from +4.8% growth in H1FY26. PAT rose 22.0% to ₹25,699 cr, though PAT margin slipped from 9.8% to 9.3%. The better quality signal is that Value of New Business (VNB, the profit expected from new policies) grew 34% to ₹6,846 cr, and VNB margin widened 470 bps to 22.3%. Weaker spots: policy count fell 2.25%, individual non-participating APE fell 6%, and Indian Embedded Value (EV) slipped 1.95% to ₹7,97,378 cr. For valuation I used P/EV, the right yardstick for life insurers, and ignored P/E. A market cap of about ₹5.0L cr against EV of ₹7.97L cr gives P/EV of roughly 0.63×, well below book embedded value. LIC is also the cheapest of its 4 listed life-insurance peers on every multiple (P/B 2.05× vs a 6.8× peer median), so I grade it cheap, even after allowing a discount for state ownership and a lower-margin product mix. The main risk to this view is that EV and individual-policy volumes are both falling while VNB margin rises, which may mean growth relies on a mix shift and could be squeezed by IRDAI's proposed commission rule changes.

Berger Paints is India's number-two decorative paints maker, with growing industrial, construction-chemical and international businesses, and it says its market share stayed stable through Q2 even as Birla Opus pushes into the market. Because paints are a consumer franchise, I graded valuation on P/E against the sector card's 30–60× band rather than against steel and metals stocks: a trailing P/E of 50.9× (38.7× forward) is fair, though top quartile within Materials (P87), and it sits below the priciest peers ASIANPAINT and PIDILITIND. The biggest risk is that management sees no easing in input costs and is relying on further price increases from November, while a new entrant makes it harder to pass costs on. Cash conversion is also very weak, with H1 CFO/PAT at 0.23x and free cash flow of -₹82 cr.

fundamental.thesis: IRCON is a state-owned railway and highway EPC contractor; about 76% of its ₹21,296 cr order book is railways, so its revenue depends on how fast it executes that book. Revenue has turned around from -21.9% YoY in Q1FY26 to +9.5% in Q1FY27 and +14.9% in Q2FY27 (about ₹2,272 cr, implied as H1 minus Q1). Profit has not followed: PAT fell 36% YoY to ₹192 cr in H1FY27, with Q2 PAT of about ₹100 cr down roughly 27%. PAT margin fell from 9.2% to 4.4% and EBITDA margin from 17.1% to 13.6% over the six periods shown. Because this is a capital-intensive order-book business, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus order cover rather than P/E. EV/EBITDA is 17.8x, and P/B is 2.0x for an ROE of only 9.1%. The order book is about 2.3x FY26 revenue and has shrunk about 11% YoY from ₹23,865 cr. Trailing P/E is 22x and forward P/E 16.5x, which looks cheap against the 28–45x industrials band. That discount is explained by thin margins, a shrinking order book and FY26 free cash flow of ₹-1,150 cr, so I grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that a shrinking order book plus weak cash conversion caps the revenue recovery while margins keep falling.

FY26 revenues grew +21.7% YoY to ₹7,701 cr (accelerating from just +4.0% in Q3FY25), with B2B driving 25.5% volume growth and PAT advancing +17.4% to ₹574 cr; critically, FY26 CFO/PAT of 1.62× confirms earnings quality, though EBITDA margin compressed 118 bps and the unverified yfinance Q1FY27 print (~+16% revenue YoY, PAT down ~17% YoY) signals a tentative growth deceleration requiring PDF confirmation. fundamental.thesis: RHI Magnesita India is one of India's leading refractories manufacturers, supplying high-temperature resistant materials primarily to steel, cement, and glass industries; it sits within the RHI Magnesita global group and commands meaningful market share in domestic installed capacity. Q1FY27 revenue grew 5.6% YoY to ₹1,014 cr — decelerating from a peak of +14.3% in H1FY26 — while PAT surged 83.2% YoY to ₹65 cr on a low base; more importantly, EBITDA margins expanded to 14.5% (vs 10.8% a year ago), recovering toward FY25 levels of 13.6% and signalling genuine operational improvement after FY26 was distorted by a ₹556 cr goodwill impairment on the RHIMIRL subsidiary. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for this capital-intensive business, the stock trades at 17.82× vs a broad-market peer median of 23.3× (P34 rank), which the system flags as fairly valued — not cheap enough to compensate for the elevated risk profile given the impairment history and debt load. The single biggest risk is the extreme financial leverage (D/E of 12.6) which, combined with revenue growth decelerating to low single digits and a brand-new MD/CEO at the helm, leaves the business highly exposed if steel/cement end-market demand softens.

RVNL is a state-owned railway EPC contractor that also takes on metro, power-transmission and overseas projects (including a recent Ministry of External Affairs award and an MoU with DVC). Its revenue depends on executing its order book, and it earns thin construction margins. Q1FY27 revenue rose 10.6% YoY to ₹4,321 cr and PAT rose 18.7% to ₹160 cr (3.7% PAT margin), the first clear pickup after a flat FY26 (revenue +2.5%, PAT -31.5%) and a weak Q1FY26 (revenue -4.0%, PAT -39.9%). One quarter of recovery does not yet prove the trend, especially with cash conversion weak (CFO/PAT of -3.44x in the latest cash-flow print) and sell-side EPS estimates cut 12.5% for FY27 and 20% for FY28 over 90 days. On the sector card's yardstick for capital-intensive order-book businesses (EV/EBITDA), the stock is expensive at 70.3x, the 95th percentile of the broad market, and its trailing P/E of 59x is well above the 28–45x Industrials range, with ROE of only 9% against a P/B of 5.2x. The stock sits near its 52-week low, but that reflects the de-rating rather than value. The biggest risks are that management misses its ~15% revenue and 15–20% PAT growth guidance, and that the ₹890 cr disputed KRCL interest receivable (roughly a full year of PAT) gets written down, with Q2FY27 results due on 13 Nov.

fundamental.thesis: Suzlon is India's largest domestic wind turbine maker, with a 6.1 GW order book (84% from PSU and commercial/industrial buyers). Growth is slowing and margins are shrinking: Q1FY27 revenue grew +22.5% YoY to ₹3,819 cr, down from +54.7% a year earlier and +42% in Q3FY26. PAT fell -5.9% to ₹305 cr, PAT margin dropped from 10.4% to 8.0%, and EBITDA margin dropped 360 bps to 15.6%. Execution growth also slowed to +14%, and the order book covers only about 2x revenue, well short of the 3x+ that would give strong visibility. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because this is an order-book industrial. At 25.7x it is about 10% above the broad-market median (P58), so it is fair, not cheap. The 25.3x trailing P/E looks low against the 28–45x Industrials range, but FY26 PAT (19% margin, including a ₹1,114 cr Q4) looks inflated by one-off tax credits, which also distorts the 40.6% ROE and 10.2x P/B. The 5.87 debt/equity figure looks inconsistent with Suzlon's historically low-debt balance sheet and should be treated as suspect data. The biggest risk is that margins keep compressing while earnings fail to turn into cash (CFO/PAT 0.38x in FY26). Analysts cut FY EPS estimates 10.6% over 90 days, and Q2 results are due on 29 Oct.

Shipping Corporation of India is a state-owned shipping company that earns most of its money from tankers (₹2,878 cr of H1 FY27 revenue at a 44% segment margin), with smaller liner, bulk-carrier and offshore businesses. Its results depend on freight rates, which go up and down with the cycle. Growth picked up sharply: H1 FY27 revenue rose 55.8% YoY to ₹4,137 cr and PAT rose 120.4% to ₹1,197 cr. Working back from the H1 and Q1 figures, Q2 FY27 revenue was about ₹2,290 cr (roughly +71% YoY) and PAT about ₹578 cr (25.2% margin), up from +40.3% revenue growth in Q1 and +3.1% for FY26. The cash backs this up, with cash from operations at 1.10x PAT in H1 against 0.82x in FY26. For valuation I used P/E and P/B, not order-book metrics, because this is a freight-rate business rather than a capital-goods order-book name. On trailing P/E of 10.65x (P7 among broad-market peers) and P/B of 1.69x the stock looks cheap, but I grade it fair: low P/Es are normal near the top of a freight cycle, and the forward P/E of 93.7x and EV/EBITDA of 35.2x do not fit with H1 EBITDA of about ₹1,975 cr, so I don't trust that part of the snapshot. The biggest risks are a fall in freight rates from today's strong Middle East-driven levels and stress at the LNG joint ventures, which led to a ₹240 cr provision and going-concern warnings from auditors. Board committees that still break SEBI listing rules and a government stake sale stuck since 2020 add to the governance risk.

fundamental.thesis: Tega Industries makes mining consumables and equipment, and its June 2026 purchase of Molycop has turned it into a much larger, heavily indebted group. Q1 FY27 revenue of Rs 1,720 cr includes only one month of Molycop, so the legacy business's +21% YoY growth is the better guide; that is a rebound from FY26 (revenue +3.2%, PAT -28.9% to Rs 143 cr) and Q3 FY26 (revenue -1.4%, PAT -63.7%), led by consumables (+36%) while equipment fell 44%, and the order book rose about 22% to Rs 1,230 cr (2.7x legacy quarterly revenue, so the reported jump from 0.68x is not like-for-like). EBITDA margin fell from 20.0% to 15.3% as lower-margin Molycop came in (13% in June), Q1 FY27 PAT is unavailable, and management guides to about 15% with synergies from Q3-Q4 FY27. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, the stock grades expensive at 51.7x (P90 against a broad-market median of 23.3x, not tight peers) with forward P/E at 48.4x, but trailing multiples and possibly EV appear to mostly pre-date Molycop, so 48.4x is the firmer evidence and the biggest risk is group debt of about Rs 11,200 cr against uncertain integration, with Q2 FY27 results due on 5 Nov 2026.

The dominant risk is that the recovery story rests on a single high-growth segment (Passenger Rail) while core Freight Rail continues contracting, and extreme leverage (D/E 25×) amplifies the downside if earnings momentum stalls in a RISK_OFF macro with sustained FII selling.

On the capital-intensive yardsticks of EV/EBITDA and EBITDA per tonne, I grade valuation fair: 12.3x EV/EBITDA is on depressed earnings, the 35.0x trailing P/E (Materials benchmark 12-22x) is distorted by one-offs, and the P19 EV/EBITDA and P15 P/B ranks are less useful because they compare against the broad market, not cement peers; the 15.7% position in the 52-week range offers some support, but this is not clearly cheap with FY EPS estimates cut about 19% in 30 days. The biggest risk is that fuel inflation and Central India dilution keep margins falling while capex of ₹3,200-3,400 cr continues, leading to further estimate cuts.

fundamental.thesis: Deepak Fertilisers is a mid-cap ammonia-chain business. It makes industrial chemicals (nitric acid, IPA, methanol), it is a leading Indian producer of technical ammonium nitrate (TAN) for mining, and it sells crop nutrition (NPK, specialty fertilisers), with large new capacity at Gopalpur (TAN) and Dahej (nitric acid) due to start in Q2 FY27. On the official filings, FY26 revenue grew 12.0% to ₹11,506 cr, but PAT fell 21.8% to ₹739 cr. Profitability has been shrinking through the year: PAT margin slid from 8.1% (H1) to 7.0% (9M) to 6.4% (full year), and EBITDA margin from 17.3% to 14.6%. The filing-extracted trend table has no Q1 FY27 revenue or PAT, and the unverified yfinance figure (PAT ₹490 cr on ₹1,886 cr revenue) looks like it may include a one-off. Treating this as a cyclical chemicals business, we judge it on EV/EBITDA: 11.1× is about half the broad-market median (bottom 15% of the market), but it is above the 5–8× the sector card calls normal for chemical cyclicals at mid-cycle. Trailing P/E of 16.9× sits inside the 12–22× Materials range, so overall we grade it fair. The forward P/E of 10.6× and analysts raising this year's earnings estimates by 43% over 30 days already assume the new plants succeed. The biggest risks are a slow ramp-up at the new plants with debt high (debt/equity about 0.76) and free cash flow negative (−₹396 cr in H1 FY26), together with raw-material squeeze from the Middle East and a falling-margin trend.

GMDCLTD is a Gujarat state-owned miner whose main business is lignite. Mining brings in nearly all its revenue (FY26 mining revenue ₹2,508 cr out of ₹2,653 cr total), and the loss-making power segment adds the rest. In Q2FY27, revenue from the official filing rose 71.2% YoY to ₹903 cr, faster than +23.8% in Q1FY27. Reported PAT fell 63.3% to ₹171 cr, but that is because Q2FY26 included a one-time ₹474 cr GST credit; without it, PAT grew about 27%. The PAT margin is 18.9%, close to Q1's 18.0% and well below FY26's 36% (which was inflated by the one-off). The quarter was strongly cash-backed: operating cash flow was 3.9x PAT and free cash flow ₹376 cr. Because this is a capital-heavy commodity miner, the right measure is EV/EBITDA, and the reported 43.9x is far above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm for cyclicals. However, that figure, the 163% dividend yield and the 4.47 debt/equity do not fit with Q1 EBITDA of ₹267 cr and the low liabilities in the segment data, so I treat them as unreliable. On the more dependable cross-check, trailing P/E of 20.6x is at the top of the 12–22x Materials range and P/B of 2.78x with 14.2% ROE is not cheap. Forward P/E (22.0x) is above trailing, which means earnings are expected to fall, so the grade is fair, not cheap, even though the stock ranks low on P/E against the broad market. The biggest risk is that the 71% revenue jump does not match the yfinance figure (₹538 cr), and it brought only modest underlying profit growth while margins shrank.

fundamental.thesis: NMDC Steel runs a single 3 MTPA integrated steel plant at Nagarnar, demerged from NMDC Ltd, and is still ramping up. The Government holds 50.79% and is looking for a strategic buyer. Revenue growth has slowed sharply from +129–179% during the ramp-up to +8.8% YoY in Q1FY27 (₹3,662 cr), but margins have turned around: EBITDA margin went from -37.9% (Q3FY25) to 7.9% (9MFY26) to 12.1% (₹442 cr), and PAT turned positive at ₹51 cr, up 97.6% YoY. Even so, the PAT margin is a thin 1.4%, the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) is only 0.17, and finance costs of ₹126 cr took about 29% of EBITDA. We use EV/EBITDA, the sector card's yardstick for steel, because P/E means little on near-zero profit (235.6x). At 11.7x the stock looks expensive against the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for steel, even though it ranks cheap (P17) against the broad market. That broad-market comparison is a fallback, not a true steel peer set. P/B of 1.05x is not a bargain when ROE is only 0.4%. The main risk is that profit stays too thin to cover heavy SBI loan repayments (₹3,177 cr outstanding, 30 quarterly instalments to 2031), with Q2FY27 results due on 12 Nov 2026 as a near-term binary event. The reported debt/equity of 35.02 is most likely a percentage (about 0.35x), which fits the loan size, so it is not a sign of extreme leverage.

fundamental.thesis: PCBL is one of the world's top three carbon black makers, with 900,000 MTPA of capacity after the Mundra specialty line was commissioned. It also owns the Aquapharm water-treatment chemicals business. The latest quarter from the filings, Q1FY27, was strong: revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹2,474 cr and PAT jumped 65% YoY to ₹155 cr, with EBITDA per tonne around ₹22,900. However, about ₹70 cr of that came from cheap inventory, and management flagged that ₹40–50 cr of it would reverse in Q2. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2 Nov have not been extracted from the official PDF yet. Unverified yfinance figures show Q2 PAT of ₹74 cr, roughly half of Q1, which fits the expected reversal and softer demand. Analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 9.8% over the last 30 days. Since this is a capital-intensive, cyclical chemicals business, I graded it on EV/EBITDA: at 17.7× it sits far above the 5–8× mid-cycle norm for cyclical chemicals in the sector card. Trailing P/E of 50.8× is well above the 12–22× Materials range, and forward P/E of 21.2× is at the top of that range, so I rate it expensive even though it looks cheaper than the broad market. The biggest risk is rising crude (around $91) feeding into feedstock costs, combined with high leverage, while volumes are weak in the near term.

fundamental.thesis: Abbott India is the Indian listed arm of Abbott. It is a branded-formulations franchise focused on the domestic market (Thyronorm, Duphaston and other women's health, gastro and chronic-therapy brands), so it is in the sector card's 'safe template' group with no US-tariff exposure. The only reliable figures are full-year FY26: revenue of ₹6,929 cr (+8.1% YoY) and PAT of ₹1,552 cr (+9.7% YoY), with a 27.7% EBITDA margin and a stable 22.4% PAT margin. Cash conversion was good but not excellent (CFO/PAT 0.85x, FCF ₹1,278 cr). The Q1FY27 yfinance row does not add up (₹932 cr revenue against a ~₹1,730 cr quarterly run-rate, and a 46% PAT margin), so I ignored it. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 have not been extracted yet, which means I cannot read the current trend. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 35.8x sits inside the 28-40x pharma range and at P52 against peers, and EV/EBITDA is 28.1x (P62), so I grade it fair. The forward P/E of 28.8x points to expected earnings growth, and the stock trades at 8.4% of its 52-week range, a better entry point if the Q2 numbers hold up. The biggest risk is that the price slide reflects a weaker Q2 or growth slowing to mid-single digits, which this stale data cannot confirm or rule out. Two of the snapshot figures are almost certainly data errors and I ignored them: a dividend yield of 201% and debt/equity of 3.6 for a company that has historically had no debt (the second may be lease liabilities or a unit mismatch).

fundamental.thesis: Eris Lifesciences is a domestic branded-formulations company focused on chronic therapies such as diabetes and cardiac care, with almost no US-tariff exposure. Revenue growth has picked up from +7.4% YoY in Q1FY26 to +11.0% in Q3FY26 and +13.0% in Q1FY27 (₹873 cr). PAT rose +20.7% to ₹142 cr, a 16.3% PAT margin. However, EBITDA grew only +6.4% and EBITDA margin slipped from 35.9% to 34.2% YoY, so the PAT growth comes from below the operating line rather than from better operations. On the healthcare yardstick of P/E cross-checked against EV/EBITDA, the stock looks fair. Trailing P/E is 31.6x, inside the 28-40x pharma range. EV/EBITDA of 18.8x is below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P37), forward P/E of 23.1x implies expected earnings growth, and the stock sits at 34% of its 52-week range. The main risks are working-capital stress and estimates being cut. The current ratio fell to 0.60 from 0.93, collections and inventory turnover both slowed, debt/equity is 0.64, and consensus FY EPS has been cut 7.7% over 90 days while 9 of 10 analysts still rate it a buy. Q2FY27 results come on 26-Oct, so the latest data is one quarter old and a binary event is three days away.

fundamental.thesis: NATCO Pharma is a midcap generics maker whose earnings lean heavily on the US (tagged US revenue of Rs 3,760 cr against FY25 total revenue of Rs 4,430 cr), with a smaller domestic business that grew about 25% in Q3 FY26 and a clean FDA note for FY26. Revenue swung from +10.8% to -7.9% (Rs 4,078 cr) between FY25 and FY26 while PAT fell 24.8% to Rs 1,418 cr and PAT margin narrowed from 42.6% to 34.8%; Q1 FY27 figures were not extracted and the quarterly rows look non-comparable, but FY27 guidance of Rs 3,300-3,400 cr revenue and about Rs 750 cr PAT implies roughly -17% to -19% revenue and -47% PAT. Using earnings-based multiples with peak profits discounted, valuation is fair rather than cheap: trailing P/E of 11.2x is far below the 28-40x pharma range but sits on earnings expected to fall sharply, while forward P/E of 19.3x (about 21x on guided PAT) is a more modest discount, and conflicting price inputs (about Rs 798 from consensus versus about Rs 884 from the 52-week position) make these multiples approximate. The biggest risk is that the remaining business and planned acquisitions cannot replace the shrinking high-margin US profit, with results due on 13 Nov 2026 and the recent rights issue (17,058,082 shares) and promoter filings still to be assessed; the 7.74 debt/equity reading may be a percentage and needs checking.

Poly Medicure is a mid-cap Indian maker of medical devices (infusion, vascular access and dialysis consumables) that sells in many countries, and it benefits from China+1 sourcing shifts in global medtech supply chains. The Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-05 but have not been extracted, and the FY26 rows in the trend table contradict each other (revenue ₹995 cr vs ₹3,076 cr, PAT margin 32.2% vs 10.8%), so I cannot reliably state the latest revenue or PAT growth rate or its direction. The only usable Q2FY27 details are qualitative: the Risor/Medistream acquisition lost ₹15.55 cr on ₹144 cr of first-half revenue, and the company has taken over Himalayan Mineral Waters, a business unrelated to medical devices that lost ₹2.69 cr. On valuation, trailing P/E of 49.6x is above the 28–40x Healthcare benchmark, while forward P/E (33.6x) and EV/EBITDA (33.8x) sit around the 70th percentile of the broad market. A P/B of 5.1x against a 10.8% ROE looks stretched, so I grade it expensive even though the peer check alone reads fair. The biggest risk is that loss-making European acquisitions and the move into an unrelated business dilute returns on capital before the core device business can absorb them, and I cannot confirm the current earnings trend without the extracted results.

fundamental.thesis: CarTrade Tech runs India's dominant online used-car marketplace across Consumer (listings), Remarketing (B2B auctions), and Classifieds (auto ads) segments, with a structurally advantaged position as organized channels continue displacing unorganised used-car trade. Q1FY27 revenue grew +16.2% YoY to ₹201 cr — decelerating from the 22–24% corridor sustained across FY26 and the ~37% seen in 9M FY25 — but PAT grew +20.6% to ₹57 cr as EBITDA margins expanded sharply from 32.7% (9M FY25) to 45.5% (Q1FY27), evidencing genuine operating leverage and a cash-backed earnings profile (FY26 CFO/PAT 1.15×). At trailing P/E 58× (P76 vs broad market), EV/EBITDA 41.4× (P83 vs peers), and P/B 5× against an ROE of only 9.8%, the stock is expensive by peer rank; the sector card argues 60–100×+ is achievable for platform models, but the forward P/E of 36.4× shows earnings acceleration is already priced in, and analyst EPS estimates have been revised up +6.8–12% over 90 days, leaving limited further re-rating catalyst. The single biggest risk is further deceleration in top-line growth at a premium multiple — in a RISK_OFF macro with FII selling and rising crude, any Q2FY27 revenue miss or guidance tone-shift could trigger the 25–40% de-rating the sector card explicitly flags for these names.

The Ramco Cements is a mid-sized, South India-focused cement maker. The sector card describes the industry as consolidating, with UltraTech and Adani holding about 45% of capacity, which leaves smaller players like Ramco competing on price. Revenue growth has picked up, from -1.0% YoY in Q1FY26 to +9.6% in Q1FY27 and +10.0% in Q2FY27 (Rs 2,466 cr). Profit has gone the other way: Q2FY27 PAT fell 48.6% YoY to Rs 38 cr, a margin of just 1.6% versus 3.3% a year ago. Q2FY27 profit also includes a Rs 4.8 cr exceptional gain and leaves out about Rs 8.6 cr of disputed mineral land tax, so underlying earnings are weaker than reported. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-heavy cement; my verdict is expensive. At 17.1x EV/EBITDA, 30.1x trailing P/E (above the 12–22x Materials range) and 2.6x book for only a 9% ROE, the stock is priced for a margin recovery the filings don't yet show. Forward P/E of 28.7x is barely below trailing. The broad-market peer ranks (P31 on EV/EBITDA) compare it with unrelated sectors, so I gave them little weight. The stock trades near its 52-week low, but that alone is not a reason to buy.

EIH runs the Oberoi and Trident luxury hotel chains, a top-tier franchise in India's premium travel market, and is adding 6 new properties (about 667 rooms) to its development pipeline. EBITDA grew only +6% to ₹208 cr, the EBITDA margin was 29.8% versus 32.3% on a standalone basis, and the headline +226% PAT jump to ₹120 cr came from one-off exceptional gains; underlying PAT grew only about 1%. Hotels need a lot of capital, so we valued EIH mainly on EV/EBITDA: 16.1x is about 31% below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P29), and a trailing P/E of 25.2x is far below the 60–100x the sector usually commands. With the stock near its 52-week low (11% of the range), we grade it fair rather than cheap, because the trailing earnings are inflated by one-offs. The biggest risks are costs rising faster than room revenue while foreign tourist arrivals stay weak, and the Q2 results due on 12-Nov, which could swing the stock either way.

fundamental.thesis: Lenskart is India's largest omnichannel eyewear retailer. It makes and sells its own frames and lenses through a big company-run store network and online, and it is a premium-consumption franchise inside Consumer Discretionary. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 32.5% YoY (per the 4 Nov press release), and PAT more than doubled to about ₹232 cr. That puts Q2 revenue at roughly ₹2,845 cr (H1 ₹5,559 cr minus Q1 ₹2,714 cr) and the PAT margin at about 8.2%, close to Q1's 8.4% and up from 5.6% in FY26. H1 earnings are cash-backed, with CFO/PAT of 1.84x and FCF of ₹365 cr. But revenue growth has actually slowed from +43.3% in Q1 to about +32.5% in Q2. The 'accelerating' trajectory flag comes from mixed period ordering and should not be relied on, and the FY26 row (₹881 cr) is clearly corrupted. I graded valuation on the card's retailer yardstick: EV/sales, EV/EBITDA and growth delivery. At 90.6x EV/EBITDA, 12.3x sales, 181.8x trailing and 95.5x forward P/E, it sits at P97–P99 against the broad market, well above even the 60–100x premium band for consumer names. The stock is at 94% of its 52-week range, and the mean analyst target of ₹718 is slightly below the current price, so this is expensive. Upward estimate revisions (+12–13% over 90 days) support the growth story but look largely priced in. The biggest risk is a de-rating: with no explicit management guidance and growth already cooling, any further slowdown at this multiple could trigger the 25–40% single-reset drawdown the sector card warns about.

Revenue growth in the trend table has slowed from +118% to +9%, and PAT margin has narrowed from 27.6% to 24.1%. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 42.5x is above the 28–40x pharma band. EV/EBITDA of 35.8x ranks in the 75th percentile of the broad market, and P/B is 7.3x. The forward P/E of 29.5x does build in an earnings recovery, so I grade it expensive, mainly on EV/EBITDA and P/E against the pharma band. The biggest risk is that the unread Q2 results confirm the slowdown, which would leave a premium multiple without growth to support it. The ₹800 cr QIP at ₹506 per share also dilutes existing shareholders and will push ROE down until the money is put to work.

Saregama is one of India's largest music-rights owners, with a big film and non-film catalogue that it earns from through streaming, licensing, and live events and video content. Q2 FY27 revenue from operations was ₹314.3 cr, up 37% YoY, adjusted EBITDA was ₹118 cr (up 39%) and PBT was ₹85.8 cr (up 43%). That is a sharp reversal from FY26, when revenue fell 15.9% and the 9M FY26 decline was 25.1%, and it comes off a soft base (H1 FY26 revenue was down 2.3%). Margins rose slightly to about 37.5% EBITDA, against 34-38% in recent periods. Because this is a content-IP business that spends heavily on catalogue, I graded it on EV/EBITDA plus P/E: 25.5x EV/EBITDA is P58 against the broad market and the 43.9x trailing P/E is P64 (about 25% above the 35.2x median), both well below the sector card's 60-100x range for consumer discretionary premium names. The 32.3x forward P/E and the 14-16% rise in earnings estimates over 90 days support earnings growth, but the stock sits at 74% of its 52-week range and the consensus target is only 2.4% above the price, so I call it fair, not cheap. The main weakness is cash conversion: FY26 free cash flow was ₹-114 cr and cash from operations was only 0.48x PAT, because content-acquisition spending is running ahead of the cash it earns back.

fundamental.thesis: CEAT is India's #4 tyre maker (global rank #4 by brand) with 51% replacement, 30% OEM, and 19% export mix, operating at 95% capacity utilisation across ~80,000 daily tyres — a capital-intensive ancillary with defensive replacement demand. Q2FY27 revenue grew a strong +26.2% YoY to ₹4,762 cr, but PAT collapsed -39.8% YoY to ₹112 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from ~13–14% (FY26/Q3FY26) to just 9.5% today — this is the defining trajectory: top-line accelerating while margins are structurally compressing, driven by commodity cost headwinds from the West Asia conflict and the Camso acquisition integration costs; the DSCR of 0.84× (below the 1.0× sustainability floor) and a current ratio of 0.67× flag tightening liquidity. Valuation looks outright cheap: EV/EBITDA at 7.4× sits at P5 vs the broad market (median 23.3×), trailing P/E of 20.2× is at P23 vs peers and -43% below market median — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock screens as cheap, but the multiple compression is warranted given the margin collapse, and forward P/E of 15.1× implies the market expects earnings recovery, which is far from assured. The single biggest risk is that commodity costs (natural rubber, crude derivatives) persist or worsen into H2FY27, keeping EBITDA margins pinned at 9–10% and preventing the earnings recovery the forward P/E demands — a second consecutive quarter of PAT decline would trigger a meaningful derating.

fundamental.thesis: JBM Auto combines a components business (Q2FY27 revenue about Rs 1,037 cr, +24.7% YoY) with a fast-growing electric bus business (about Rs 548 cr, +21.8% YoY, 24% reported market share and 578 buses delivered in the quarter). Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, valuation is expensive at 24.0x for a 12.2% EBITDA margin, even though that is only P52 against a broad-market peer set rather than close auto peers; trailing P/E of 64.8x is well above the 18-30x OEM range, P/B of 12.7x is P89, and forward P/E of 31.0x assumes earnings roughly double. The biggest risk is that growth keeps needing debt-funded capital while thin margins and weak cash generation (H1FY27 operating cash flow Rs 143 cr, free cash flow Rs 14 cr, net debt Rs 2,732 cr) leave little room for error; the 14.0% dividend yield looks like a data error and was ignored, and the '2.7x H1 revenue' debt figure is wrong because Rs 2,732 cr is about 0.9x H1 revenue.

fundamental.thesis: BBTC is the Wadia Group's holding company with a controlling stake in Britannia Industries plus tea/coffee plantations and auto-electrical components — P/E comparison to pure FMCG operators is structurally misleading, and the correct yardstick here is P/B plus EV/EBITDA (sector card conglomerate guidance), not the 40–65× FMCG P/E benchmark. Using yfinance (Q1FY27 official PDF data is absent from the trend table), revenue grew +5.9% YoY to ₹2,959 cr, decelerating from +8.7% in Q1FY26, while PAT margin expanded sharply to ~9.7% (from 5.1% in Q1FY26) — though that expansion likely includes volatile Britannia dividend and investment income rather than structural operating improvement (note H1FY26 CFO/PAT was −0.02×, a poor cash-conversion signal for the operating businesses). On EV/EBITDA of 3.06× (P0 in broad market) and P/B of 1.42× with the stock at 14.6% of its 52-week range, BBTC appears deeply cheap by any metric — but a structural holding-company discount of 30–50% is normal and persistent, and the extreme D/E of 16.57 with US 10Y at 5.29% and rising is an offsetting overhang that explains why the discount exists. The biggest risk is that debt is likely collateralised against the Britannia stake, meaning a sustained FII-driven de-rating of Britannia under the current RISK_OFF regime could trigger a collateral squeeze at the BBTC level, amplifying downside disproportionately.

Olectra Greentech is a midcap maker of electric buses (Mobility division, about 86% of Q1FY27 revenue, partnered with BYD) and composite polymer insulators (Energy division), which puts it at the centre of India's public-transport electrification. On the official Q1FY27 filing, revenue grew 65.7% YoY to Rs 575.5 cr, faster than +10.6% a year earlier and +28.3% for FY26. But PAT rose only 2.4% to about Rs 27 cr: finance costs nearly doubled (Rs 12.0 cr to Rs 23.6 cr), EBITDA margin fell from 16.1% to 12.7%, and PAT margin fell from 7.5% to 4.6%. Earnings are also not turning into cash well: FY26 cash from operations was only 0.58x PAT and free cash flow was negative (Rs -55 cr). I graded valuation on trailing P/E because the EV/EBITDA (1066x), Debt/Equity (30.8) and Price/Sales (58x) figures in the snapshot look like data errors. At 56x trailing P/E, the stock is well above the 18-28x Auto OEM range, at the top of the 28-45x Industrials range, and in the top quarter of the broad market (P75 on P/E, P73 on P/B at 8.1x), so it is expensive. The 27.9x forward P/E assumes a sharp profit recovery that the latest quarter has not yet shown. The biggest risk is the Q2FY27 results on 9 Nov 2026: if margins keep shrinking or interest costs keep rising, a stock priced for growth could be cut down to a lower multiple.

Bikaji Foods is India's third-largest ethnic snacks maker, best known for bhujia, and it is growing its distribution quickly: it added 19.2k outlets in Q2 to reach 3.9 lakh, and its core markets grew 17.5%. Profit growth is weaker still: Q1FY27 PAT rose only +1.6% YoY to ₹59 cr, and PAT margin fell from 9.4% to 7.7% over the trend window. The key FMCG measure, volume growth, was only about 6.2% in H1FY27 against 12.8% value growth, down from 9.5% in FY26, so much of the growth is coming from price and product mix rather than real demand. I graded valuation on trailing P/E against the FMCG sector norm of 40–65×: at 54.9× trailing (39.3× forward) and 34.5× EV/EBITDA it sits inside the band, so it is fair, not cheap. The stock is near its 52-week low, and while all 11 analysts rate it a buy, their FY earnings estimates have been cut 5.5% over 90 days, a common pattern before a stock re-rates lower.

fundamental.thesis: Hexaware is a mid-cap IT services firm reporting on a January–December year, with its strongest growth currently in Healthcare & Insurance (+31.9% YoY) and Manufacturing & Consumer (+31.1% YoY), while Travel & Transportation is shrinking (-14.5% YoY). fundamental.thesis: Torrent Power is a vertically integrated private utility operating licensed electricity distribution across Gujarat, Maharashtra, and UP (4.29M customers, India's lowest distribution-loss record) alongside 6.6 GW of gas, coal, and renewable generation capacity, with a further ~8.9 GWp under development including renewables, pumped storage, and coal. Q1FY27 revenue grew a modest +2.8% YoY to ₹8,124 Cr — decelerating from +10.0% in Q2FY26 and +4.3% in Q3FY26 — while Total Comprehensive Income fell 13.5% YoY to ₹639 Cr; PAT margins have contracted from ~10.5% (FY25) to ~8.3% (FY26) and an estimated ~7.9% in Q1FY27 as higher finance costs from the ₹3,632 Cr Nabha Power acquisition (June 2026, 1.4 GW supercritical coal with long-term Punjab PPAs) weigh on reported PAT despite stable EBITDA margins at ~20%. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business (per sector card instruction), 15.03× vs a broad-market median of 23.3× places TORNTPOWER at the P25 cheapness rank; the trailing P/E of 30.25× sits above the 10–18× utility sector benchmark, but the forward P/E compressing to 23.1× signals the market is already pricing in earnings recovery from the commissioning pipeline, yielding a fair overall valuation grade. The CFO resignation (August 2026) is a governance red flag at a sensitive execution juncture for a midcap, compounded by elevated leverage from Nabha and LNG supply disruptions already suppressing thermal plant performance.

Zensar is an RPG-group mid-tier IT services firm with two businesses, Digital Services and Cloud Infrastructure, and it has a net cash position of ₹326 cr. Revenue is growing a little faster: H1FY27 revenue was ₹3,094 cr, up 10.2% YoY, compared with +7.5% to +8.7% through FY26, and Cloud Infrastructure grew 12.3%. Profit is not keeping up. H1 PAT of ₹374 cr rose only 2.7%, and PAT margin fell to 12.1% from 13.6% in FY26. Some of that drop is a one-off ₹24.9 cr Labour Code provision, but excluding it margin is still only about 12.9%. Cash conversion has also weakened, with CFO/PAT at 0.73x and only ₹22 cr of free cash flow because capex took up 8% of revenue, which is unusually high for an IT services firm. On valuation it looks cheap: trailing P/E is 12.6x against an IT sector band of 22–30x, EV/EBITDA is 8.2x (P7 across the market), and forward P/E of 11.2x is below trailing. Treat that discount with care, though. The stock is near its 52-week low, analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by about 1.2–1.4% over 90 days, and the market may be pricing in AI-driven shrinkage of mid-tier IT revenue. The feed also has several conflicting numbers: the Q1 revenue figure differs between sources, the Q2FY26 row is off by a factor of 10, and D/E of 1.68 and a 351% dividend yield contradict the net-cash position. So read the cheap grade with somewhat less confidence.

fundamental.thesis: Emami is a mid-sized Indian FMCG company selling ayurvedic personal care and healthcare brands such as Navratna, BoroPlus and Zandu, and it is now buying its way into digital-first brands (60% of IncNut Digital, majority control of Axiom Ayurveda). In H1 FY27, revenue rose +24.9% YoY to ₹2,127 cr, compared with -5.2% in H1 FY26 and -0.8% for FY26. Domestic revenue rose +31.7% while exports fell -3.9%. Much of this jump comes from the two acquisitions, and no volume growth figure was disclosed, so we cannot tell how much is real underlying demand. PAT fell -9.0% to ₹284 cr, PAT margin dropped from 18.4% to 13.1%, EBITDA margin dropped from 25.6% to 22.6%, and finance costs more than doubled to ₹11.7 cr. fundamental.thesis: Cohance Lifesciences is an Indian CDMO/API platform (formerly Suven Pharmaceuticals) serving global pharma innovators across Pharma CDMO, API+, Sapala nucleic-acid specialty chemicals, and Formulations — a niche franchise currently navigating a sharp operational trough driven by post-merger NJ Bio consolidation, Pharma CDMO order phasing, and Specialty Chemicals destocking. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue declined 23.1% YoY to ₹422 cr (decelerating sharply from +12.5% in Q1FY26 and extending the -13.1% full-year FY26 decline), with Pharma CDMO down 38.7% YoY, NJ Bio contributing an EBITDA loss of ₹328 mn, and PAT swinging to ₹-45 cr (-176% YoY); EBITDA margins imploded 2,220bps to 2.2%, though gross margins held at 71.5% and FCF remained a healthy ₹106 cr — indicating the trough is volume/timing-driven rather than structural margin destruction, and management has guided Q1FY27 as the floor with H2FY27 YoY recovery. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per sector card guidance for a capital-intensive CDMO, the stock trades at 39.3× (P81 vs broad-market peers, 68% premium to median 23.3×), expensive on any normalised basis; trailing P/E of 88.6× (P91, distorted by the trough PAT) and forward P/E of 38.9× still sit well above sector Pharma medians of 28–40×, while sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 25.5% in the last 30 days — suggesting the recovery the market is paying for is actively being revised downward. The biggest risk is binary: an active FDA Warning Letter at the Nacharam FDF facility, if not resolved swiftly, could trigger customer qualification audits across the CDMO business precisely when the recovery pipeline depends on securing and delivering new orders against a backdrop of dangerously high Debt/Equity of 9.93.

I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a hospital business with heavy capital needs: at 26.1x it is only about 12% above the broad-market median (P59), and the forward P/E of 36.5x against a trailing 51.3x shows earnings growth is expected, so the stock looks fair, not cheap. fundamental.thesis: Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands is a mid-cap branded apparel company that owns Louis Philippe, Van Heusen, Allen Solly and Peter England, plus a smaller emerging-brands portfolio. It sells through 3,434 stores, 40,500 multi-brand outlets, 6,800 shop-in-shops, e-commerce and wholesale. fundamental.thesis: Patanjali Foods is India's largest edible oils company (formerly Ruchi Soya), with a fast-growing FMCG overlay spanning biscuits, nutrition, and home/personal care under the Patanjali brand — but edible oils still account for roughly 70%+ of revenues, making this a commodity-FMCG hybrid rather than a pure compounder, and that matters critically for how to frame the valuation. Q1FY27 delivered record revenue of ₹11,337 cr (+29.3% YoY, accelerating from +20.9% in Q2FY26) and PAT of ₹336 cr (+86.1% YoY), but underlying quality is deteriorating: gross margin compressed from 15.26% (Q2FY26) to 13.42% (Q1FY27), EBITDA margin fell from 6.2% to 4.8%, and PAT margin contracted to 3.0% — a persistent multi-quarter contraction signal that runs counter to the top-line acceleration. At trailing P/E 25.43×, the stock screens cheap versus the FMCG sector benchmark of 40–60×, but the discount is structurally warranted by the commodity-heavy business mix; EV/EBITDA of 25× (P55 vs broad-market peers) and P/E peer rank of P32 both point to fair value rather than genuine mispricing, and the sector card's own caution — 'cheap FMCG usually means a structural problem' — applies directly here. The overriding risk is extreme balance sheet leverage (D/E 21.3×) combined with negative FCF (CFO/PAT −1.13× in Q2FY26) — at a 5.29% US 10Y yield and with PAT margins at 3%, any commodity cost spike or interest burden increase could rapidly destroy earnings entirely.

Ramkrishna Forgings makes forged and machined parts, mainly for commercial vehicles, rail and global auto platforms, and has subsidiaries in the USA and Mexico. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 36.3% YoY to ₹2,621 cr and PAT rose to ₹117 cr from ₹2 cr, with EBITDA margin up from 14.6% to 18.1%. Revenue growth has improved quarter by quarter, from -4.5% (H1 FY26) to +19.8% (Q1 FY27) to +36.3% (H1 FY27), but much of that comes off a weak base hit by a ₹42 cr provision on bad receivables, and the yfinance quarterly figures (₹734 cr in Q2) do not match the filing-based table. Because this is a capital-intensive business, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA: 20.0x is P42 against the market and about 14% below the median, and a forward P/E of 27.7x sits at the top of the 18-28x auto-ancillary range. The 148x trailing P/E is inflated by the depressed base, so overall valuation looks fair, and with the price at the consensus target (₹697) there is little room left. The biggest weakness is cash: operating cash flow was only ₹41.5 cr in H1 (0.35x PAT) against ₹390 cr of capex, so free cash flow was -₹349 cr, inventory is building and finance costs take 4.5% of revenue. Return on equity is weak at 2.3%.

Intellect Design Arena is a mid-cap banking and insurance software maker. It sells licences, platform subscriptions and maintenance (AMC) to more than 500 financial institutions in 62 countries. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹855 cr, up 13.0% YoY, and growth has slowed over the trend window from +36.2% (Q2 FY26) to +20.6% (Q1FY27) to +13.0%. On the main IT yardstick, trailing P/E is 31.2×, just above the 22–30× sector range. The forward P/E of 18.4× and EV/EBITDA of 17.0× sit well below the broad-market median (P31–P43), so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that the heavy AI spending (the MSOCK platform) keeps squeezing margins while revenue growth keeps slowing, so revenue growth stops turning into profit growth.

IGL is the main city gas distributor in Delhi NCR, selling CNG to vehicles and piped gas (PNG) to homes and businesses. It is still adding volume: total volumes grew 6.9% YoY to 9.86 MMSCMD in H1 FY27, CNG rose 7.5% and domestic PNG rose 11.5%. Profits, however, have collapsed. H1 FY27 revenue grew 21.4% to ₹10,654 cr, but gas purchase costs jumped 39%, EBITDA margin fell from 12% to 3%, and PAT dropped 71% to ₹211 cr (a 2.0% margin). Q2 alone was much worse: EBITDA was negative ₹31 cr and PAT was about ₹26 cr, down roughly 93% from ₹386 cr a year earlier. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E, as suits a capital-intensive utility. On those, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 15.4x (inside the 10–18x utilities range), EV/EBITDA is 10.5x and the stock sits around the 12th–15th percentile of the market. But both figures are based on trailing earnings that are falling fast, and analysts have cut current-year EPS estimates by 50–59% in 90 days. So I grade it fair, and the low multiples may be a value trap. The biggest risk is that IGL cannot raise CNG and PNG prices to cover higher gas costs (in a politically sensitive Delhi market, with crude near $91 and rising), so margins stay crushed.

fundamental.thesis: Inox Wind is India's leading wind turbine manufacturer and turnkey EPC player, serving utility-scale developers including public-sector clients such as IOCL, with a growing O&M contract base (₹11,212 cr unbilled) that provides some recurring revenue visibility. The multi-quarter trajectory is deteriorating on every dimension — revenue growth has decelerated sharply from +103.7% (FY25) through +41.7% (H1FY26) to +23.6% (Q4FY26), with Q1FY27 PAT down 34.1% YoY to ₹64 cr from ₹97 cr; PAT margins have contracted from 12.8% (Q1FY26) to 9.2% (Q4FY26), and EBITDA is also softening (₹210 cr vs ₹220 cr Q1 prior year). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials (per sector card), at 17.8× vs sector median 23.3× the stock screens at P33 and appears modestly discounted, but this apparent cheapness is materially misleading — ~₹9,884 cr in contingent liabilities (₹4,306 cr EPCG customs-duty exposure + ₹5,578 cr SECI bank guarantees invoked) equate to ~64% of market cap and are absent from the EV, justifying a FAIR grade at best. Sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 43% in 90 days while all 6 analysts retain BUY — a classic pre-derating divergence — and binary resolution of the EPCG/SECI liabilities on an already-extreme D/E of 20.63× is the make-or-break risk.

fundamental.thesis: J.K. Cement is a mid-sized cement maker that is also building a paints business through its subsidiary JK Maxx Paints. A new ₹130 cr, 75,000 KLPA plant in Telangana is funded from a ₹600 cr paints budget. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 20.3% YoY to ₹4,032 cr, but PAT fell 15.3% YoY to ₹275 cr. EBITDA margin has slid from 19.5% (H1FY26) to 17.0% and PAT margin from 7.5% to 6.8%, so volume growth is not reaching profits. The Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-10-24 but have not been extracted yet, and the yfinance quarterly rows (₹513 cr revenue) are clearly inconsistent with the filings and were ignored. On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business: 18.8× is below the broad-market median of 23.3×, but trailing P/E of 40.8× is far above the 12–22× Materials benchmark. Forward P/E of 25.6× depends on an earnings recovery that analysts are actively cutting (FY EPS estimates down 9.3% over 90 days), so I grade it expensive, even though cement usually commands a premium and the stock sits at 13.7% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is further margin compression in a crude-up, weak-rupee, risk-off environment, made worse by spending on paints, a segment the sector card describes as structurally broken by Birla Opus's entry.

Cholamandalam Financial Holdings is a holding company (formerly TI Financial Holdings) whose value comes mainly from its stake in Cholamandalam Investment & Finance (CIFCL), a large vehicle- and asset-backed lender, plus the Chola MS general insurance business (CMSGICL) and a small risk-services JV. In Q2FY27, total consolidated income grew 18.8% YoY to ₹11,388 cr and reported PAT rose 25.2% to ₹1,520 cr (13.3% margin). The lender is clearly driving results: CIFCL disbursements were ₹35,872 cr and its PAT rose 41% to ₹1,630 cr. Group revenue growth has been easing slowly, from +21.8% in Q1FY26 to about +19% now, and the Q2 PAT figure looks like it may be on a different basis from the parent-attributable ₹806 cr shown for Q1, so the margin trend is hard to read. The sector card says to value holding companies on their discount to the value of what they own, not on P/E. That NAV discount cannot be worked out from the data given, so I used P/B and P/E against peers as a stand-in: trailing P/E is 10.8x, forward P/E 8.0x and P/B 1.86x, in the cheapest 5–16% of the peer set. Because holding companies normally trade 40–60% below the value of their stakes, I call this cheap but not a big mispricing. The main drag is insurance: CMSGICL lost ₹120 cr in Q2 because of natural-catastrophe claims and high motor own-damage claims, its H1 profit fell to ₹8 cr from ₹165 cr, and full-year EPS estimates have been cut 6.1% over the last 30–90 days.

Against that, the insurance arm is losing money, earnings estimates were cut 6%, sentiment is neutral with stale guidance, and the stock is bouncing into resistance (%B 0.94) while still below its 200-day average. fundamental.thesis: 3M India is the listed Indian arm of 3M and makes diversified industrial, safety, transportation & electronics, healthcare and consumer products. It sells products rather than working through an order book, and it has net cash of about ₹420 cr. Revenue is still growing but more slowly: Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹1,452 cr, up 14.7% YoY, down from +19.0% in Q1. PAT fell 17.2% YoY to ₹158 cr as EBITDA margin compressed for a third straight period, from 20.3% in FY26 to 17.6% in Q1 and 16.1% in Q2. Management blamed a weaker rupee and higher input costs linked to the Middle East, and Q1's ₹233 cr PAT included a ₹73 cr one-off gain from a land sale. Since the business is not capital-intensive or order-book driven, I graded valuation on trailing P/E checked against EV/EBITDA: 64× P/E and 36.5× EV/EBITDA are well above the 28–45× industrials range and at P77–P96 against the broad market (P/B 20.9×). That makes it expensive even after allowing for the 42× forward P/E, the strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 3.1×) and the expected ~₹110 cr Thermo Fisher payment. The biggest risk is that a premium-multiple stock keeps losing margin: if the rupee and input-cost pressure persist, earnings growth falls behind sales growth and the stock could lose its premium. The healthcare transition to Solventum and Thermo Fisher also clouds that segment's future revenue.

fundamental.thesis: Sonata Software is a mid-cap IT company with two parts: international IT services, focused on Microsoft and Dynamics work and AI-led modernisation, and a large, low-margin domestic business that resells Microsoft and other software. The latest results we have from official filings are from Q1FY26 (June 2025), when revenue was ₹2,965 cr (+17.3% YoY) and PAT was ₹109 cr (+3.5% YoY), giving a thin 3.7% PAT margin, down from 4.2% in FY25. Underneath that, constant-currency services growth turned negative (-2.4% vs +3.9%), utilisation slipped and attrition rose to 16%, while deal wins (TCV) improved to $105M. The Q2FY27 results filed on 5 November 2026 have not been extracted yet, so this view is stale by several quarters. On price, the trailing P/E of 15.6x (forward 12.7x) and EV/EBITDA of 12.2x are well below the 22–30x IT sector range and near the bottom fifth of the broad market, so the stock grades cheap on P/E and EV/EBITDA (P/E is meaningful for this asset-light, profitable business). The biggest risk is that it is a value trap: sell-side EPS estimates have been cut about 7–8% over 90 days, and AI-driven price deflation in legacy services could keep shrinking growth and margins.

fundamental.thesis: Adani Energy Solutions is India's largest private power-transmission company, with about 30% share of recent transmission bids, 29,802 circuit km of lines, a Mumbai distribution business, a fast-growing smart-meter business and a newly consolidated energy-trading platform. In H1 FY27, revenue rose 47.5% YoY to ₹19,787 cr and PAT rose 137% to ₹2,600 cr, a 13.1% PAT margin, after Q1 FY27 grew revenue 42.4% and PAT 124%. Two caveats apply to that growth: the H1 figures restate prior periods to include the energy-trading platform, and they count ₹4,961 cr of construction revenue (SCA, up from ₹3,692 cr). The extracted H1 rows also conflict (₹14,351 cr vs ₹19,787 cr). We grade valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/B against ROE, the yardstick for capital-intensive utilities: EV/EBITDA of 25.1x, P/B of 7.2x on a 9.7% ROE and trailing P/E of 81.7x are far above the 10–18x utilities range, and the stock sits at 89.5% of its 52-week range. Analysts raising FY EPS estimates by about 16% in 30 days and a ₹87,222 cr transmission order book give good visibility, but the price already assumes flawless delivery. The main risks are leverage and execution: debt/equity is 1.84x, net debt is ₹41,067 cr, free cash flow is negative (₹-3,185 cr in H1), capex guidance is ₹21,000–25,000 cr a year, and Adani group news can move the stock regardless of results.

fundamental.thesis: Reliance Power is a midcap private generator with about 5.3 GW operating, mostly coal (Sasan ultra-mega plant with a long-term contract, running at about 92% load factor, plus Rosa). Only 145 MW is renewable, and another 4.8 GW of renewable and hydro capacity is stuck in the pipeline. In Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue grew 3.8% YoY to ₹1,956 cr and PAT rose 44.9% YoY to ₹65 cr, a thin 3.3% PAT margin. This follows a FY26 loss of ₹337 cr, which came after a ₹38,160 cr asset write-down. The 'accelerating' revenue signal is mostly noise across quarters: growth has gone +12.2%, ~+1.5%, +0.5%, +3.8%, so the real picture is low-single-digit growth with no management guidance. I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-heavy power company, plus P/B. At 8.3x EV/EBITDA (P8 vs the broad market) and 0.69x book, the stock looks cheap. But ROE is negative at -2.1% and interest costs eat about 18% of revenue, so a large part of the discount is a fair price for balance-sheet and governance risk, not a clear mispricing. The biggest risk is group solvency: auditors have flagged going-concern doubts, subsidiary RSTEPL has defaulted on about ₹2,296 cr of debt, and lenders have called a parent guarantee of about ₹1,842 cr for SMPL, which is now in insolvency proceedings. Any of these could wipe out the equity value that the low P/B seems to offer.

fundamental.thesis: Aster DM Healthcare runs hospitals and, after the merger with Quality Care India closed on 1 July 2026, is one of India's largest hospital platforms: 38 hospitals and 10,840+ beds across 27 cities under the Aster, CARE, Evercare and KIMS brands. In Q2 FY27, its first full quarter as a merged company, revenue rose 19.0% YoY to ₹2,829 cr and normalised PAT rose 34% to ₹281 cr, a 9.9% margin. Occupancy improved 335 bps to 68%, patient volumes grew 12% and ROCE rose to 23%. This is only one clean quarter, though, and the YoY base may not be fully like-for-like after the merger, so a multi-quarter trend can't be confirmed yet. For a capital-intensive hospital business, EV/EBITDA is the right yardstick: at 45.9x the stock is about 97% above the broad-market median of 23.3x (P87). Trailing P/E of 123x is at P97, it trades at 85% of its 52-week range, and analysts cut FY EPS estimates by 8.9% in the last 30 days. Taken together, the stock looks expensive. The biggest risk is that merger integration or a slowdown in occupancy gains falls short of the growth already priced in.

drivers: Management kept FY27 guidance unchanged ('guidance reiterated, no change'). The agenda covers merger integration, 4,170+ new beds with a preference for brownfield expansion, and a focus on ROCE. They expect 'continued margin improvement, stronger cash generation'.
FY26 results were solid: revenue up 12% YoY, EBITDA up 17% to Rs. 947 Cr, margin steady at 20.4%, and ROCE up 330 bps to 22.8%.
Risks: bed occupancy fell from 65% to 61%, material cost is still high at 21.4% of revenue, and integrating the merged brands (Aster, CARE, KIMSHEALTH, Evercare) could go wrong.

fundamental.thesis: Anupam Rasayan makes custom-synthesis specialty chemicals for agrochem, pharma and personal-care customers, and has now moved into finished medicines by buying a 50.07% controlling stake in Bliss GVS Pharma. Growth is slowing fast: Q2 FY27 revenue was a record Rs 821 Cr, but that is only +11% YoY, down from +35% in Q1 FY27 and +149% in Q2 FY26. H1 FY27 revenue was Rs 1,489 Cr (+21%) and PAT Rs 116 Cr (+10%), so profit is growing more slowly than sales. EBITDA margin improved to about 25% from 19% a year ago, but PAT margin has stayed flat at about 7.7–7.8%, which suggests interest, depreciation and minority interest are absorbing the gains. Specialty chemicals trade above commodity materials, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus P/B and ROE. On that basis the stock is expensive: EV/EBITDA is 32.6x against 5–8x for mid-cycle chemical cyclicals and 23.3x for the broad-market median (P68). Trailing P/E is 83.7x (P89), and P/B of 4.4x is backed by only 5.8% ROE. The forward P/E of 42x already assumes earnings roughly double. The biggest risk is that this optimism is not met: FY earnings estimates have been cut 22% over 90 days, free cash flow was negative in FY26 (Rs -221 Cr), and integrating Bliss GVS brings execution risk.
